slide_text: Dictionaries A dictionary maps keys to values — like an index at the back of a book. You look up a key instantly, regardless of how many entries exist. Quick Check — Dict vs List for Counting You used a dictionary to count words. Could you have used a list of pairs instead? What would be the main drawback? A. Lists can't store pairs — only single values B. It would work identically with no drawback C. Finding whether a word already exists would require scanning the entire list each time — much slower for large texts D. Lists can't be sorted

fragments.text: Answer: C. A list of pairs works, but to check if a word is already there you'd need to walk through the whole list every time — that gets very slow as the text grows. A dictionary jumps straight to the right entry.

Part 6: Inventing Hashing (Why Dicts Are Fast) You've used dictionaries all chapter without asking the awkward question: is instant even if holds a million keys. A list would have to check entries one by one. How does a dict jump straight to the right spot? The answer is an idea you're about to invent: turn the key into a number , and use that number as a position.

Letters Are Already Numbers Python exposes each character's numeric code: is , and goes back to . Write returning the position of a lowercase letter in the alphabet — → 0, → 1, ... → 25 — using (no lookup tables!). Hint If is 97 and is 98, then subtracting from any letter's code gives its position: .

A Number for Any String One letter is easy. For a whole string, the simplest recipe: add up the character codes . That gives a big number; to turn it into a position , take the remainder when dividing by the number of slots available. Write = (sum of of every character) . The result is always a valid index between and — exactly what you need to pick a slot in a list of buckets. [code block] Hint Use a loop: , then . Finally .

The Collision Run this before reading on: [code block] Both give . Of course — they're anagrams (Part 2 of this chapter!), so they contain the same letters, and addition doesn't care about order. Two different keys landing in the same bucket is called a collision , and a hash that collides for every anagram is a bad hash. The fix: make position matter. Weight each character by where it sits: Write using the weighted sum, and confirm the anagram pair now separates. [code block] Hint 1 gives you pairs where is the position (0, 1, 2, ...) and is the character. Hint 2 Replace the simple sum with: inside the loop. The makes position matter.

The Same Trick at Data-Center Scale You just invented how a dict works inside: Hash the key to a bucket index — one arithmetic step, no searching. Go directly to that bucket. Collisions are unavoidable (infinitely many strings, finitely many buckets), so each bucket keeps a short list to check — a few items, not a million. That's why takes the same amount of time whether the dict holds ten keys or ten million. Computer scientists call this O(1) — meaning "constant time", independent of the data size. Now zoom out. A big website can't fit a billion users on one database server; it splits them across many. Which server holds user ? Same invention: hash the key. With numeric IDs the hash is just the remainder. Write returning , then check the test's fairness experiment: hashing 10,000 users across 7 servers should load every server almost equally. [code block] Think about it (no code): if you add an 8th server, becomes — which users are now on the wrong server? (Almost all of them! Real systems use smarter techniques to avoid reshuffling everyone. Python dicts face the same problem when they grow: they resize and re-hash every key.)

Quick Check — What Happens on a Collision? You built a hash function that converts a string to a number, then uses modulo to pick a bucket. What happens when two different keys hash to the same bucket (a collision)? A. The second key silently replaces the first — data is lost B. Python raises an error and refuses to insert C. The bucket stores both key-value pairs, and lookup checks each one — still fast on average if collisions are rare D. The hash function automatically picks a different bucket

fragments.text: Answer: C. Each bucket keeps a short list of all key-value pairs that landed there. On lookup, Python scans that short list. As long as collisions are rare (the hash spreads keys evenly), the list stays tiny and lookups remain fast.
